## Upcrossings

Let $(y_n)$ be a sequence of real numbers and fix an interval $[a,b]$ with
$a<b$. Define

$$
T_1 = \min\{ n : y_n \le a \},
\qquad
T_2 = \min\{ n > T_1 : y_n \ge b \}.
$$

The interval $[T_1, T_2]$ is called an **upcrossing** of $[a,b]$. For
$k \ge 2$ define

$$
T_{2k-1} = \min\{ n > T_{2k-2} : y_n \le a \},
\qquad
T_{2k} = \min\{ n > T_{2k-1} : y_n \ge b \}.
$$

The **number of upcrossings** of $[a,b]$ by the finite sequence
$(y_0,\dots,y_n)$ is denoted $U_n(a,b;y)$, and the **total number of
upcrossings** of $[a,b]$ by the infinite sequence is

$$
U(a,b;y) := \lim_{n\to\infty} U_n(a,b;y).
$$

**Downcrossings** are defined similarly by reversing the inequalities and
swapping $a$ and $b$.

:::{.theorem data-title="Upcrossings and Convergence"}

If a sequence of real numbers $(y_n)$ diverges, then there exist rational
numbers $a<b$ such that $U(a,b;y)=\infty$.

:::

`\begin{proof}`
If $(y_n)$ diverges, then $\liminf y_n < \limsup y_n$, so there are rational
numbers $a<b$ with $\liminf y_n < a < b < \limsup y_n$. Then $y_n \le a$ for
infinitely many $n$ and $y_n \ge b$ for infinitely many $n$, so $(y_n)$
crosses $[a,b]$ upwards infinitely often, that is $U(a,b;y)=\infty$.
`\end{proof}`

This reduces convergence of a sequence to finiteness of $U(a,b;y)$ for the
countably many rational pairs $a<b$, which is how the upcrossing inequality
is used to prove the [[martingale-convergence-theorems]].

## Upcrossing Inequality

:::{.theorem data-title="Upcrossing Inequality"}

Let $(X_n, \mathcal{F}_n)$ be a [[martingale-theory|submartingale]], $a<b$,
and let $U_n(a,b;X)$ be the number of upcrossings of $[a,b]$ by
$X=(X_n)$ up to time $n$. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}[U_n(a,b;X)] \le \frac{1}{b-a}\,\mathbb{E}[(X_n-a)^+].
$$

:::

`\begin{proof}`
Put $Y_n = (X_n - a)^+$. This is a nonnegative submartingale (a convex
nondecreasing function of a submartingale), and upcrossings of $[a,b]$ by $X$
are upcrossings of $[0,b-a]$ by $Y$, so $U_n(a,b;X) = U_n(0,b-a;Y)$.

Define the predictable process $C_1 = \mathbb{1}_{\{Y_0 = 0\}}$ and, for
$n \ge 2$,

$$
C_n = \mathbb{1}_{\{C_{n-1}=1\}}\mathbb{1}_{\{Y_{n-1} < b-a\}}
+ \mathbb{1}_{\{C_{n-1}=0\}}\mathbb{1}_{\{Y_{n-1} = 0\}}.
$$

That is, we start betting when $Y$ hits $0$ and stop once it exceeds $b-a$.
Each completed upcrossing of $[0,b-a]$ contributes at least $b-a$ to the
transform $(C\bullet Y)_n = \sum_{k=1}^n C_k(Y_k - Y_{k-1})$, and an
unfinished final stretch contributes at least $0$ since $Y \ge 0$. Hence

$$
(b-a)\,U_n(0,b-a;Y) \le (C\bullet Y)_n.
$$

Since $1-C$ is predictable and nonnegative, $((1-C)\bullet Y)$ is a
submartingale null at $0$ (see [[martingale-theory]]), so
$\mathbb{E}[((1-C)\bullet Y)_n] \ge 0$. Therefore

$$
\mathbb{E}[(C\bullet Y)_n]
= \mathbb{E}[Y_n - Y_0] - \mathbb{E}[((1-C)\bullet Y)_n]
\le \mathbb{E}[Y_n - Y_0] \le \mathbb{E}[Y_n],
$$

and combining the two displays gives
$(b-a)\,\mathbb{E}[U_n(a,b;X)] \le \mathbb{E}[(X_n - a)^+]$.
`\end{proof}`
